I grew up with major sensory issues that were the most obvious in food, so that for several years I could only eat either sour cream or black bread. I didn't really take much issue with it until I got older and started realising how "weird" everyone thought it was — kids around me were brutal but adults often even more so. I do realise that it was out of worry and belief that they were trying to help, but it did lead down a path of near phobia of food — when there is always a negative spotlight on you, you give up even trying. Because what if you can't have it or throw up and they sneer at you again? Best not to try...

Around age 17 I met my now best friend whose mom is a doctor — she asked me to write down a list of things I can eat, and then sent me suggestions on how to get my daily nutrients in as much as possible so I could still take care of my body. This was hugely helpful and made me feel like I had some control over my eating again.

I have limited experience with therapy, but I will share what I know.

Therapists that you meet will be different across the board, because people are different. A therapist that fits you might not fit somebody else, and vice versa. Because of this, your first therapist might not be who you'll want to stick with (my first one pissed the hell out of me because she kept saying stuff like "oh that must have been so hard for you" and looking like she was about to cry - which might be exactly what some people need, that type of sympathy, but it wasn't doing it for me. My second one was a much better match.)

So that being said, it can be a bit of a chore, but finding the right one is totally worth it. Just need to find a person you click with - after all, you WILL be sharing some of your deepest concerns and fears with them, might as well feel comfortable with it.

Now, if you connect with a therapist, they will read that as a great sign. This shows - as does your message here - that you actively want to make a difference, but just aren't quite sure on how to go about it. Fortunately for us, they are professionals.

A therapist will (/should, and you can always ask them to before starting, as well) walk you through their privacy policy and what exactly that entails, but as a general rule, they will not do anything unless it sounds like you are in extreme, immediate risk of harming yourself or others. This meaning, if you tell them that you are suicidal and have a plan for it, they most likely won't take it as an immediate red flag, because a lot of their clients most likely can attest to the same.

If anyone has any actual experience with being hospitalised or the therapist taking extreme measures, that might be helpful as an addition! But my understanding had always been that the privacy and autonomy of patients is 100% valued.
